title: Acute Asthma Exacerbation in Children: Inhaler Technique and Oral Steroid Discharge Plan

evidenceAudit.scope: Paediatric acute asthma assessment, emergency treatment, inhaler technique and oral-steroid discharge plan; SINA 2024 Section 10 and Box 10.3. Medicine-pathway restructure on 2026-10-18: medicines regrouped into branches, steps and give-all vs choose-one options; no dose, source or clinical claim was re-checked.
findings: Rewritten from the pasted draft using the Saudi Initiative for Asthma (SINA) 2024 child acute-asthma pathway.
Every included dose, threshold and disposition step is traced to SINA 2024 Section 10 or Box 10.3.

pathophysiology.summary: Acute airway inflammation, bronchial smooth-muscle constriction and mucus increase expiratory airflow obstruction. Air trapping can increase work of breathing and ventilation–perfusion mismatch. Exhaustion with falling air entry can precede respiratory failure.
keyMechanisms: Airway inflammation narrows the bronchial lumen.
Bronchospasm causes variable expiratory airflow obstruction and wheeze.
Mucus and air trapping increase work of breathing.
Severe airflow obstruction can cause hypoxaemia; exhaustion and a silent chest are danger signs.

symptoms: Wheeze or worsening shortness of breath.
Reduced activity; in children younger than 2 years, lethargy or poor feeding.
physicalSigns: Tachypnoea, increased work of breathing, reduced air entry or wheeze.
Assess oxygen saturation, ability to speak or feed, and level of alertness.
redFlags: Acute distress, inability to complete a few words in one breath, or poor response to short-acting beta-2 agonist (SABA) at home require urgent medical care.
Silent chest, exhaustion, cyanosis, altered consciousness or worsening oxygenation require immediate senior and paediatric critical-care assessment.
precipitants: Viral upper respiratory tract infection commonly precedes attacks.
Poor controller adherence, incorrect inhaler technique, tobacco smoke or vaping exposure, and known environmental triggers.

differentials.condition: Viral bronchiolitis in children younger than 2 years
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: A common winter differential; assess age, clinical pattern and response rather than assuming asthma.
Fever above 39°C with focal reduced breath sounds and crackles supports pneumonia and is an indication to consider chest radiography.
Asymmetric signs, sudden onset or a poor response to maximal treatment warrants assessment for an alternative diagnosis or complication.

ruleIn.targetCondition: Acute asthma severity or alternative diagnosis
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Document initially and after treatment to guide treatment intensity and disposition.

ruleIn.targetCondition: Acute asthma severity or alternative diagnosis
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Saturation below 92% or deterioration indicates hypoxaemia
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Give oxygen as needed to maintain saturation ≥92%; reassess with the clinical score.

ruleIn.targetCondition: Acute asthma severity or alternative diagnosis
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Reduced air entry, silent chest, exhaustion or altered consciousness
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Identify life-threatening deterioration and obtain urgent paediatric critical-care help.

ruleOut.targetCondition: Acute asthma severity or alternative diagnosis
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Abnormal ventilation or acid-base status in severe asthma not responding to maximal therapy
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Not routine; use for severe non-response requiring Intensive Care Unit (ICU) consideration.
ruleOut.normalValue: Adult arterial pH 7.35–7.45; arterial carbon dioxide partial pressure 35–45 mmHg (4.7–6.0 kPa); local paediatric laboratory ranges apply

ruleOut.targetCondition: Acute asthma severity or alternative diagnosis
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Focal consolidation, pneumothorax or another alternative diagnosis
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Do not image routinely; consider for fever >39°C with focal signs, suspected pneumothorax, diagnostic uncertainty, disproportionate hypoxaemia or severe non-response.
ruleOut.normalValue: No focal consolidation, pneumothorax or other acute thoracic abnormality

clinicalManagement.title: ABCDE survey with concurrent correction
actions: Work through Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability and Exposure in order, and correct each abnormality concurrently as it is found: do not wait for the full survey, investigations or a diagnosis before treating a life-threatening problem, and call for senior help early.

Airway: look, listen and feel for obstruction; open it with a neutral head position (head tilt in older children) or jaw thrust, suction secretions, use an oropharyngeal airway if unconscious and call for expert paediatric airway help if it cannot be kept patent.

Breathing: count respiratory rate, measure SpO2, check recession, grunting, nasal flaring and air entry; if SpO2 is below 94% give [💊 Oxygen | 10–15 L/min via reservoir mask | Inhaled | Continuous | Until SpO2 94–98%, then titrate to target] and treat life-threatening chest problems as they are found.

Circulation: check heart rate, capillary refill and blood pressure, attach a monitor and secure IV access if the attack is severe (PRAM 8–12); if shocked give [💊 Sodium chloride 0.9% | 10 mL/kg | IV or IO bolus over 10 minutes | Reassess after each bolus; repeat if still shocked | Until perfusion restored].

Disability: assess responsiveness (alert, voice, pain, unresponsive), pupils and posture, and measure capillary glucose; if glucose is below 3 mmol/L give [💊 Glucose 10% | 2 mL/kg | IV or IO bolus | Repeat after 10 minutes if glucose remains below 3 mmol/L | Until glucose 3 mmol/L or above]; look for seizure activity.
Exposure: expose the child to examine fully while preventing heat loss; check temperature, skin (rash, bruising, wounds) and abdomen, then cover again.

clinicalManagement.title: Immediate assessment and first hour
clinicalManagement.timeframe: At presentation and every 20 minutes during the first hour
actions: Record vital signs, oxygen saturation and PRAM.
Give [💊 Oxygen | 10–15 L/min via reservoir mask | Inhaled | Continuous | Until SpO2 92% or above] when required.

For initial home treatment the written plan uses [💊 Salbutamol | 2–4 puffs | Inhaled by metered-dose inhaler (MDI) with spacer | Every 20 minutes for up to three doses | Initial home management only]; seek medical advice promptly even if improved.
In the emergency department, use the PRAM-directed pathway and reassess after treatment.

clinicalManagement.title: Moderate or severe attack
actions: For PRAM 4–7 use weight-based [💊 Salbutamol | under 20 kg: 5 puffs by MDI/spacer or 2.5 mg nebulised; 20 kg or more: 10 puffs by MDI/spacer or 5 mg nebulised | Inhaled | Every 20 minutes, directed by the PRAM pathway | First hour and reassessment] and add [💊 Ipratropium bromide | 4 puffs by MDI/spacer or 250 micrograms nebulised | Inhaled | Every 20 minutes for the first hour | First hour only].

After the first SABA dose, when indicated, give [💊 Prednisolone | 1–2 mg/kg (maximum 20 mg under 2 years, 30 mg at 2–5 years, 60 mg at 5–12 years) | Oral | Once daily | 3–5 days total] or [💊 Dexamethasone | 0.6 mg/kg (maximum 16 mg) | Oral | Second dose the following day | Two-day course].

For PRAM 8–12, establish IV access, monitor closely, consider continuous nebulised [💊 Salbutamol | 2.5 mg (under 20 kg) or 5 mg (20 kg or more) per nebulisation, repeated back to back | Inhaled, continuous nebulisation | Back to back doses | Until PRAM improves] and contact paediatric intensive care.

clinicalManagement.title: Discharge plan and follow-up
clinicalManagement.timeframe: After sustained response; observe one hour after the last bronchodilator when the pathway specifies
actions: Discharge only if PRAM ≤3 after observation and the child is clinically stable.

Provide [💊 Salbutamol | 2–4 puffs | Inhaled by MDI with spacer | Every 4–6 hours for 24 hours, then as needed | 24 hours, then as needed], complete the oral steroid course ([💊 Prednisolone | 1–2 mg/kg (maximum 20 mg under 2 years, 30 mg at 2–5 years, 60 mg at 5–12 years) | Oral | Once daily | 3–5 days total] or [💊 Dexamethasone | 0.6 mg/kg (maximum 16 mg) | Oral | Second dose the following day | Two-day course]), continue the inhaled corticosteroid until the next clinic review if indicated, and supply a written action plan.
Observe the child and caregiver demonstrating one-puff-at-a-time spacer use: shake the inhaler, seal mouthpiece or mask, actuate one puff, allow several normal breaths, then repeat as prescribed.
Arrange clinic review within one week.

regimens.patientGroup: Children with an individual asthma action plan
regimens.route: Inhaled by metered-dose inhaler (MDI) with spacer
regimens.frequency: Every 20 minutes for up to three doses
regimens.duration: Initial home management only; seek medical advice promptly
adjustments: Use a spacer; use the child’s individual action plan and local protocol.
monitoring: Symptoms, work of breathing and response after each dose.
contraindications: Hypersensitivity; use clinical caution with significant tachyarrhythmia.

regimens.patientGroup: Children weighing under 20 kg or 20 kg and above
regimens.dose: <20 kg: 5 puffs by MDI/spacer or 2.5 mg nebulised; ≥20 kg: 10 puffs by MDI/spacer or 5 mg nebulised
regimens.frequency: As directed by PRAM pathway; titrate MDI dose to response
adjustments: Use weight band and local nebuliser/oxygen protocol.
monitoring: PRAM, oxygen saturation, heart rate and clinical response.
contraindications: Hypersensitivity; use clinical caution with significant tachyarrhythmia.
regimens.branch: Emergency department — moderate or severe attack

regimens.indication: Moderate or severe attack during first hour
regimens.patientGroup: Children managed by the PRAM pathway
regimens.dose: 4 puffs by MDI/spacer or 250 micrograms nebulised
regimens.frequency: Every 20 minutes for the first hour only; maximum three doses
adjustments: Use local device equivalence and infection-control policy.
monitoring: PRAM, oxygen saturation, heart rate and anticholinergic adverse effects.
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to ipratropium or atropine derivatives.
regimens.branch: Emergency department — moderate or severe attack
regimens.useWhen: Moderate or severe attack during the first hour

regimens.indication: Systemic steroid after first SABA dose when indicated
regimens.patientGroup: Children with moderate or severe attack
regimens.dose: 1–2 mg/kg; maximum 20 mg if under 2 years, 30 mg at 2–5 years, and 60 mg at 5–12 years
adjustments: If oral treatment is not tolerated or the child is critically ill, use the local paediatric emergency protocol and seek senior advice.
monitoring: Clinical response, vomiting and glucose when clinically indicated.
contraindications: Hypersensitivity; assess infection risk while treating the acute attack.
regimens.branch: Emergency department — moderate or severe attack

regimens.indication: Alternative oral systemic steroid course when selected by the treating clinician
regimens.frequency: A second dose the following day when an oral steroid course is used
adjustments: Choose one systemic-steroid regimen; do not combine routinely with prednisolone outside the pathway.
monitoring: Clinical response, vomiting and behavioural adverse effects.
contraindications: Hypersensitivity; assess infection risk while treating the acute attack.

medicationPlan.note: Doses are from SINA 2024 Section 10. SFDA registration was not independently verified in this task; check the SFDA register and hospital formulary before prescribing.

branches.label: Home — individual asthma action plan
branches.entryCriteria: Child with acute bronchospasm at home and an individual asthma action plan

branches.label: Emergency department — moderate or severe attack
branches.entryCriteria: Child with a moderate or severe asthma attack managed by the PRAM pathway

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Score 1–3 mild, 4–7 moderate, and 8–12 severe; obtain at initial assessment and after treatment.

teaching.scope: Paediatric acute asthma discharge and inhaler technique.
learningObjectives: Use PRAM at assessment and reassessment.
Give a written action plan and timely follow-up.
pitfalls: Routine chest radiography, blood gas testing and antibiotics are not indicated for a typical responding attack.
Do not discharge without observing caregiver and child inhaler-spacer technique.
keyPoints: A worsening score, silent chest, exhaustion or poor response requires escalation.
The discharge plan includes short-term SABA instructions, completion of oral steroid when prescribed, action plan, inhaler technique and clinic review.

patientEducation: Give a written asthma action plan.
Demonstrate and observe MDI/spacer technique before discharge.
Explain when to seek urgent medical care: distress, inability to speak a few words in one breath, or poor SABA response.
lifestyleAndDiet: Avoid tobacco smoke, vaping exposure and known triggers.
No special diet is recommended in the SINA acute-asthma pathway.
mdtReferrals: Paediatric emergency team; paediatric intensive care for severe deterioration or PRAM 8–12.
Asthma or primary-care clinic for follow-up.
dischargeCriteria: Clinically stable with a caregiver able to demonstrate spacer technique and follow the written plan.
